comments.author: @maficstudios
comments.text:
The piece you're missing is that the amount of money that these companies need to keep going is enormous, and that money's availability is predicated on the idea that there is a short-term ROI.  So if investors realize that it's not there - that's where the bubble bursts.  They pull their money.  Now companies don't have the megabucks they once had, and may not be able to survive.  It doesn't impact the progress, but some of the IP could be consumed/lost, there's a diaspora, which can, in turn, slow things down.

Because if AGI needs 10 trillion of compute, and none of the companies have those bucks, it can delay the advent of ... whatever ... indefinitely.  Not that more progress can't happen, or won't happen, it's just less "certain" as a consequence of the deflation in available capital.

comments.text:
Yeah in the EU there is the no TDM rule that if companies specifically say their content should not be used for Text data mining then it is illegal to use it without permission.  The TDM (Text and Data Mining) rule in the EU is primarily governed by the Directive on Copyright in the Digital Single Market (CDSM). This directive includes two main exceptions for TDM practices:
Article 3: This exception allows text and data mining for scientific research by research and cultural institutions, ensuring that these activities are lawful and do not infringe copyright rights.   Articie 4: This exception permits text and data mining by anyone, but requires that rightholders have the right to 'contract-out' their works for commercial purposes.   The EU aims to balance innovation in data-driven technologies with the rights of authors and rightholders, ensuring that TDM practices are conducted responsibly and legally.   So for   commercial purposes it isn't fair use.   I would wonder if this would force  more publishers to base their businesses in the EU where their copyright is protected from unauthorized datamining by ai companies for commercial purposes.   expressly reserved by their right holders in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means ...' 
(Article 4, Copyright Directive). This is known as the opt-out exception. Stakeholders have been debating 
the definition of ‘machine-readable’ and the duration for which reproductions of works can be kept. For 
‘machine-readable’, GPAI providers support the adoption of an easy-to-access standardised file such as 
robot.txt.            So it seems that companies like google that operate in the EU will be breaking the law if they mine data that they are informed isn't wanted to be mined by that party it would be a violation of EU Law. if used for commercial purpose.

Bubble talk aside, Google released a paper about 6 months ago on distributed AI training that would greatly democratize AI and increase its worldwide. 

The basic idea is, building powerful models without needing powerful data centers. Small entities (countries with poor digital infrastructure, small companies, individual people, etc) can use the approach in the Google paper to create frontier adjacent AI models using data and compute from around the world, and then consolidate it into a model. 

This is the path being taken by small startups flower ai and vana, they were covered in an article in wired. 

Bottom line, i think Google has laid the groundwork for AI to explode in use and be accessible for almost anyone. AI isn't in a bubble, but the high cost data center centric approach might be.

Lol.  AI is bubble 100%.  These advances seem so amazing blah blah blah.  But.  In the end, how will anyone make money off this stuff?

AI is a massively democratizing tool.  While the leaders have advantage now, it is very easy to replicate them for minimal costs after the advancements have been made.  My prediction is that AI will be a huge asset to business and humanity as a whole, but it will be a utility.  It will not make these leading AI companies rich in and of themselves.  

1.) It's too easy to copy first of all.  So in the long run, people won't be willing to pay high prices for the agents etc etc.  They would simply opt for the cheap ones that are just as good as the expensive ones.  The cheap ones would be carbon copies of the "premium" ones, with more or less stolen R&D. 

2.) And second of all, it must be accessible to be used.  If it's going to be accessible, it cannot be expensive.  If it cannot be expensive, how are any of these companies going to make profits?  Yep exactly. 

So in the end, it will be used in all aspects of industry and personal life, but it will be like a wrench or a screwdriver or a QR code.  It's going to improve human life, but not improve AI corporation profit margins.  

This seems obvious to me, I am not sure why no one else thinks this.
